source: CARDI (2011), "Series on: Rice Cultivation Environment Status in Cambodia / Soil Group Classification / Key Characteristics of 10 Rice Varieties / Simple Seed Purification Method" (Khmer, 25pp, funded by CAVAC/ACIAR, 1st printing 2011); CARDI (2011), "Handbook of Integrated Techniques for Increasing Wet-Season and Dry-Season Rice Productivity" (Khmer, 50pp, funded by CAVAC/ACIAR, foreword by H.E. Chan Sarun, Minister of Agriculture, dated 26 August 2011)
text: Impure seed stock is a major, correctable cause of yield loss: CARDI states that growing seed that is not pure can cut yield by 10–30%, produces less whole (unbroken) milled rice and more broken grain, sells for a lower price, and — critically — can turn an aromatic or soft-cooking variety into a harder-cooking, non-aromatic-tasting rice at the table because off-type plants mixed into the seed lot show up in the harvested grain and the cooked rice. A 2011 CARDI trial with 66 farmer households found that switching to purified seed of the same variety raised yield from a baseline around 500 kg/ha to about 670 kg/ha of additional paddy, an average gain of roughly 630 kg/ha (about 24%), equivalent to roughly an extra 630,000 riel of paddy value per hectare (2011 prices) compared with growing on farmer-retained seed of unknown purity. Because Cambodia's seed companies could not yet supply certified seed of all traditional varieties farmers wanted in 2011, CARDI recommends farmers maintain their own small 'seed purification plot' each season using a simple do-it-yourself method: Step 1 — work out how much seed you need (e.g. a 1-hectare field typically needs 20–30 kg of seed for broadcasting). Step 2 — pick the plot size for the purification nursery by yield: if your own field yielded, say, 3,000 kg/ha in the past, that is 30 kg per are (100 m²), so a nursery of at least 1 are (100 m²) is enough to produce the 30 kg of seed needed for 1 hectare — pick the best-performing patch of your own field to harvest from. Step 3 — set aside seed for this purification plot: soak/parboil the grain you intend to use for seed, then hand-select only grains that are uniform in size and color to the amount you need (e.g. 1 kg of seed for 1 are of nursery). Step 4 — choose a nursery site 10 m² per kg of seed, near a water source, easy to walk around and inspect, away from streetlights (which attract night-flying pests); prepare the soil to a fine tilth, avoiding weedy fields where old shattered seed from a previous crop could re-germinate and contaminate the plot; keep the seedbed well weeded. Step 5 — prepare and transplant the purification plot itself into clean, fine soil in rows of 2–3 seedlings per hill, with proper row spacing (unlike a broadcast field, row-transplanting is essential here so off-types are easy to spot and remove); irrigate, weed, and fertilize normally. Step 6 — after establishment, walk the plot and remove (rogue out) any off-type hill at least 3 times: at tillering (20–30 days after transplanting, removing hills growing out of line or visibly different from the rest); at flowering (removing hills that flower 3–5 days earlier or later than the rest, or with a different panicle/grain shape or color, cutting them off at the base); and at ripening (removing hills that ripen unevenly, with a different panicle color, different grain shape/size/color, or a different plant height than the surrounding crop). Step 7 — harvest only when at least 90% of grains are mature: at least the upper half of the panicle golden-yellow and the lower half turning golden, with fully filled grains at the panicle tip already straw-colored. Step 8 — thresh/beat out the grain separately from any other seed lot, taking care not to mix varieties, and winnow it clean. Step 9 — sun-dry the seed on a raised mat or tarpaulin (not directly on bare ground) to a thickness of 2–3 cm, turning it regularly until fully dry. Step 10 — store the finished seed in a sealed plastic bag with the air pressed out, placed inside a second sack, kept apart from eating rice in a dry location free of rats, and clearly labelled with variety name and harvest date.
caveat: This is a varietal-purity maintenance technique (roguing off-types from one's own seed stock across three growth stages), not a laboratory germination-rate test — the source title's Khmer phrase translates literally as 'seed purification/selection method', which could be confused with germination testing; flagging this distinction for anyone indexing by title. Numeric yield-loss and trial figures (10-30% loss from impure seed; +24% from purification) are as reported by CARDI and were not independently re-derived.
